subject: Animal Husbandry
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 1½-hour practical paper of four compulsory questions (60 marks); school candidates work with real specimens, tools, feeds and parasites, while private candidates sit a test of practical work. Questions ask you to identify specimens, draw and label them, state uses, functions and maintenance, and carry out simple calculations such as ration formulation, dosage and production records.

practicals.title: Identifying animal products and by-products
practicals.topic: Practical: products and by-products of farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify common farm animal products and by-products, state their uses and calculate the dressing percentage of a slaughtered animal.
safety: Wear gloves when handling raw hides, blood and dung, which may carry germs such as anthrax spores or Salmonella.
Wash hands with soap and water after the practical.
Do not taste any specimen.
procedure: Arrange the specimens on labelled trays, separating main products (meat, milk, eggs, honey) from by-products (hides, skins, horns, hooves, bones, blood, feathers, dung).
Examine each specimen with the naked eye and a hand lens; note colour, texture, smell and any distinguishing feature.
Name the animal from which each specimen was obtained.
State at least two uses of each specimen (e.g. hides for leather and ponmo, bone meal as a mineral feed supplement, dung as manure or biogas feedstock).
Weigh a live goat before slaughter and the dressed carcass after removing the head, feet, skin and offal; record both masses.
Calculate the dressing percentage and enter all observations in a table: specimen, source animal, product/by-product, uses.
practicals.expectedObservations: Hides are thick and heavy (cattle) while skins are thin and light (goat, sheep); feathers show a central shaft with vanes; horn is hard, keratinous and hollow at the base; bone meal is a whitish powder; poultry dung is greyish-white with brown portions. A goat usually dresses out at about 45–50 %.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Dressing percentage = (carcass mass ÷ live mass) × 100. Worked example: a goat weighing 25 kg alive gives a 12 kg carcass. Dressing % = 12 ÷ 25 × 100 = 48 %. The remaining 13 kg (52 %) is made up of the skin, head, feet, blood, gut contents and offal, many of which are useful by-products.
precautions: Weigh the animal after a short fast so that gut contents do not inflate the live mass.
Zero the scale before each weighing.
Keep specimens dry and labelled to avoid mixing them up.
sourcesOfError: Variable gut fill in the live animal.
Moisture loss from the carcass before weighing.
Scale not zeroed.
commonMistakes: Calling skin from a cow a 'skin' instead of a 'hide'.
Listing meat or milk as by-products.
Dividing live mass by carcass mass, giving a value above 100 %.
examTips: Give the source animal and two distinct uses for each specimen — vague uses such as 'for money' earn no marks.
Always show the formula, substitution and unit (%) for dressing percentage.
Distinguish product (main purpose of keeping the animal) from by-product (secondary).

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a by-product rather than a main product of cattle?
checkQuestions.explanation: Hides are secondary materials obtained after slaughter; beef, veal and milk are the main products.

checkQuestions.q: A pig weighing 80 kg alive gives a 56 kg carcass. Its dressing percentage is
Bone meal is used in livestock feeds mainly as a source of
checkQuestions.explanation: Bone meal supplies the minerals calcium and phosphorus.

checkQuestions.q: Feathers are processed into feather meal, which is a source of
checkQuestions.explanation: Hydrolysed feather meal is a protein (keratin) feedstuff.

practicals.title: Drawing and labelling external parts of farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify farm animals by their external features and to draw and label the external parts of a named ruminant and of the domestic fowl.
materials: Live goat or cow restrained on the school farm (or clear photographs)
Charts of breeds (e.g. White Fulani, N'Dama, Red Sokoto goat, West African Dwarf goat, Large White pig)
safety: Restrain animals properly with a halter or by holding the legs and wings of birds; stand to the side of cattle, never directly behind.
Wash hands after handling animals.
procedure: Restrain the animal calmly so that its whole side view can be seen.

Observe and name the external parts: muzzle, poll, horn, ear, neck, withers, back, loin, rump, tail, hock, hoof, dewlap, udder or scrotum, flank and brisket for the ruminant; comb, wattle, beak, ear lobe, hackle, saddle, sickle feathers, shank, spur and toes for the fowl.
Measure the body length of the animal (point of shoulder to pin bone) with a tape.
Draw an outline of the side view, about 10–15 cm long, with clean single lines.
Label the parts using ruled, parallel label lines that do not cross, and write labels horizontally.
Give the drawing a title and calculate and state the magnification.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ruminants have split (cloven) hooves, a hairless moist muzzle and often horns and a dewlap; the fowl has a comb, wattles, scaly shanks and a beak with no teeth. Breeds differ in colour, horn shape and size (e.g. the White Fulani has large lyre-shaped horns and a hump).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Magnification = drawing length ÷ actual length. Worked example: a goat measures 60 cm from shoulder to pin bone; the drawing of the same length is 12 cm. Magnification = 12 ÷ 60 = ×0.2 (the drawing is one-fifth natural size).
precautions: Draw from the specimen in front of you, not from memory.
Keep proportions correct — measure before drawing.
Use a sharp pencil; do not shade.
sourcesOfError: Animal moving while being measured.
Tape not held along the body line.
commonMistakes: Arrows instead of label lines.
Labelling the hock as the 'knee'.
Forgetting to state the magnification or giving it without the '×' sign.
examTips: Marks are given for a title, clarity of outline, correct proportions and each correctly placed label.
Magnification below 1 is correct for large animals — write it as ×0.2, not 5.
Learn two distinguishing features of each common Nigerian breed.

checkQuestions.q: Which external part is found on the fowl but not on the goat?
checkQuestions.explanation: Wattles are fleshy outgrowths below the beak of fowls.

checkQuestions.q: A cow 180 cm long is drawn 9 cm long. The magnification is
The prominent ridge between the shoulder blades of cattle is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The withers are at the top of the shoulders.

checkQuestions.q: The White Fulani breed of cattle is easily recognised by its
options: white coat and large lyre-shaped horns
checkQuestions.explanation: White Fulani cattle are white with long lyre-shaped horns and a hump.

practicals.title: Internal organs of the domestic fowl and ruminant stomach
practicals.topic: Practical: internal organs and their functions in farm animals
practicals.aim: To dissect a freshly slaughtered fowl, identify its digestive, reproductive and excretory organs, compare them with the ruminant stomach, and relate structure to function.
materials: Ruminant stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) from an abattoir
safety: Cut away from your body and keep fingers clear of the scalpel blade.
Wear gloves; dispose of offal by burying or in a covered bin.
Disinfect the board and instruments afterwards.
procedure: Pluck the feathers from the abdomen, lay the bird on its back and pin the wings and legs to the board.
Make a shallow cut through the skin from the vent to the neck, then open the body cavity carefully without piercing the gut.

Identify, in order, the oesophagus, crop, proventriculus, gizzard, duodenum with pancreas, small intestine, caeca, large intestine and cloaca; also the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys and (in a hen) the ovary and oviduct.
Uncoil the gut, measure the length from oesophagus to cloaca and the body length (beak to vent).
Open the gizzard and note the grit and the thick muscular wall.
Examine the ruminant stomach: identify the four compartments and note the papillae of the rumen, the honeycomb of the reticulum, the leaves of the omasum and the glandular abomasum.
Draw and label the fowl's digestive system and state the function of each organ.
practicals.expectedObservations: The crop is a thin-walled bag that stores food; the gizzard has thick muscular walls containing grit for grinding; there are two blind caeca; there is a single cloaca. The ruminant stomach has four chambers, the rumen being by far the largest; the pig has a single simple stomach.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Gut length : body length ratio. Worked example: intestine (oesophagus to cloaca) = 160 cm; body length = 40 cm; ratio = 160 ÷ 40 = 4 : 1. A long gut relative to body length allows more time for digestion and absorption.
precautions: Use a fresh specimen to prevent organs from decaying.
Do not cut the gut while opening the body cavity, as contents will obscure the organs.
Measure the gut without stretching it.
sourcesOfError: Stretching or coiling of the intestine during measurement.
Organs displaced during dissection.
commonMistakes: Confusing the proventriculus (glandular stomach) with the gizzard.
Saying the fowl has teeth or a bladder.
Naming the reticulum as the 'true stomach' — it is the abomasum.
examTips: Functions must match organs exactly: crop – storage and softening; gizzard – grinding; proventriculus – secretes gastric juice.
Know that the abomasum is the true (glandular) stomach of ruminants.
Drawings of the gut should show the organs in the correct sequence.

checkQuestions.q: In the fowl, food is ground with the help of grit in the
checkQuestions.explanation: The muscular gizzard grinds food using grit.

checkQuestions.q: The true glandular stomach of a ruminant is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The abomasum secretes gastric juice like a simple stomach.

checkQuestions.q: A bird has a gut 150 cm long and body length 30 cm. The ratio of gut to body length is
Which organ in the fowl is the common opening for faeces, urine and eggs?
checkQuestions.explanation: The cloaca receives the gut, urinary and reproductive tracts.

practicals.title: Distinguishing ruminants from non-ruminants
practicals.aim: To distinguish ruminant from non-ruminant farm animals by their teeth, stomach and feeding behaviour, and to estimate the share of stomach capacity taken by the rumen.
apparatus: Measuring cylinder (1 L) or graduated bucket
materials: Skull or jaw of a goat/cow
Skull or jaw of a pig
safety: Handle fresh tissues with gloves.
Clean and disinfect spillages of stomach contents.
procedure: Examine the upper jaw of the goat skull; note the absence of upper incisors and the hard dental pad.
Examine the pig skull; note upper and lower incisors and canines (tusks).
Observe live goats resting and record whether they chew the cud.
Tie off the openings of each compartment of the ruminant stomach and fill each with water to estimate its capacity; record the volumes.
Compare with the single compartment of the pig stomach.
Tabulate the differences between ruminants and non-ruminants.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have a dental pad instead of upper incisors, chew the cud and have a four-chambered stomach in which the rumen is the largest. Non-ruminants (pig, rabbit, fowl) have a simple stomach (or crop and gizzard in birds) and do not chew the cud.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Percentage capacity of rumen = (rumen volume ÷ total stomach volume) × 100. Worked example: total stomach capacity 150 L, rumen 120 L. Rumen share = 120 ÷ 150 × 100 = 80 %. This large fermentation vat is why ruminants can digest fibrous roughage with the help of microbes.
precautions: Tie compartments tightly to prevent leakage between chambers.
Read the cylinder at eye level.
sourcesOfError: Stretching of the stomach wall as it is filled.
Leakage of water between compartments.
commonMistakes: Classifying the rabbit or horse as ruminants (they are hind-gut fermenters, not ruminants).
Saying ruminants have no incisors at all — they have lower incisors.
examTips: Give paired differences (ruminant v. non-ruminant) in a table for full marks.
Name at least two examples of each group from Nigerian farms.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a ruminant?
checkQuestions.explanation: Sheep chew the cud and have a four-chambered stomach.

checkQuestions.q: Ruminants lack upper incisors and have instead a
checkQuestions.explanation: The hard dental pad works against the lower incisors.

checkQuestions.q: If the rumen holds 36 L of a 45 L goat stomach, its percentage share is

practicals.title: Tools and equipment for managing farm animals
practicals.topic: Practical: tools and equipment used in management of farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify tools and equipment used in housing, brooding, feeding, identification, debeaking, castration, dehorning, incubation and milking, state their uses and maintenance, and calculate the number of feeders and drinkers needed for a flock.
safety: Carry sharp tools with points down and never leave them on the floor.
Disconnect electrical equipment (debeaker, incubator) before cleaning.
procedure: Examine each tool and note its parts and the material it is made of.
Name each tool and state the management practice it is used for.
Demonstrate correct handling (e.g. holding the Burdizzo with both handles, loading an elastrator ring).
State two maintenance practices for each item (cleaning, disinfecting, oiling moving parts, sharpening, proper storage).
Calculate the number of feeders and drinkers needed for a given flock size using the recommended allowances.
Record name, use and maintenance in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each tool has a characteristic shape: the Burdizzo has long handles and blunt crushing jaws; the elastrator has four prongs that stretch a rubber ring; the debeaker has a heated blade; the egg candler is a box or torch with a light and a hole for the egg.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Number of equipment = flock size ÷ birds per unit. Worked example: 500 broilers; allowance 1 tube feeder per 25 birds and 1 fountain drinker per 50 birds. Feeders = 500 ÷ 25 = 20; drinkers = 500 ÷ 50 = 10.
precautions: Disinfect castration and dehorning tools between animals to prevent infection.
Store tools in a dry place to prevent rust.
Calibrate drenching guns before use.
sourcesOfError: Allowances differ with bird age and equipment size, so check the manufacturer's guide.
commonMistakes: Confusing the Burdizzo (crushes the spermatic cord) with the elastrator (rubber ring).
Writing 'cleaning' as the only maintenance practice for every tool.
examTips: Specific uses earn marks: 'used to crush the spermatic cords in bloodless castration' not 'for castration'.
Maintenance should suit the tool — oil hinges, sharpen blades, disinfect after use.
Round up the number of feeders or drinkers to a whole number.

checkQuestions.q: The Burdizzo is used for
checkQuestions.explanation: It crushes the spermatic cords without breaking the skin.

checkQuestions.q: How many fountain drinkers are needed for 750 birds at 1 drinker per 50 birds?
The egg candler is used to
checkQuestions.explanation: Light shining through the egg shows the developing embryo or a clear infertile egg.

checkQuestions.q: Which maintenance practice is most important for an elastrator after use?
options: Washing, disinfecting and oiling the hinge
checkQuestions.explanation: It has no blade; hygiene and lubrication keep it working.

practicals.title: Egg candling, fertility and hatchability
practicals.aim: To candle incubated eggs to detect fertile, infertile and dead-in-shell eggs, and to calculate fertility and hatchability percentages.
apparatus: Egg candler or bright torch in a dark room
safety: Handle eggs gently to avoid cracking or shaking the embryo.
Do not keep eggs out of the incubator for more than a few minutes.
procedure: Set clean, fertile-looking eggs in the incubator at about 37.5 °C and 55–60 % relative humidity and turn them at least three times daily.
On day 7–10, take a tray to a dark room and hold each egg's broad end against the candler.
Classify each egg: fertile (spider-like blood vessels with a dark spot), infertile ('clear'), or dead embryo (blood ring or dark blot without vessels).
Remove infertile and dead eggs and record the numbers.
Return fertile eggs quickly; stop turning on day 18 and transfer to the hatcher.
Count chicks hatched on day 21 and calculate fertility and hatchability.
practicals.expectedObservations: Fertile eggs show a network of blood vessels radiating from a dark embryo and an air cell at the broad end; infertile eggs look clear like fresh eggs; early dead embryos show a blood ring.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Fertility % = fertile eggs ÷ eggs set × 100; hatchability of fertile eggs = chicks hatched ÷ fertile eggs × 100; hatchability of eggs set = chicks ÷ eggs set × 100. Worked example: 300 eggs set, 30 clear at candling, 243 chicks hatched. Fertile = 270; fertility = 270 ÷ 300 × 100 = 90 %; hatchability (fertile) = 243 ÷ 270 × 100 = 90 %; hatchability (set) = 243 ÷ 300 × 100 = 81 %.
precautions: Candle in a dark room so that the internal features are visible.
Wash hands before handling hatching eggs.
Avoid temperature fluctuations in the incubator.
sourcesOfError: Thick or brown shells make embryos hard to see.
Mistaking early dead embryos for clear eggs.
commonMistakes: Dividing by eggs set when the question asks for hatchability of fertile eggs.
Turning eggs during the last three days.
examTips: State which base you are using (eggs set or fertile eggs) in hatchability calculations.
Know the incubation period: chicken 21 days, duck 28 days, turkey 28 days, quail about 17 days.

checkQuestions.q: A 'clear' egg on candling is
checkQuestions.explanation: No embryo or blood vessels have developed.

checkQuestions.q: 200 eggs are set; 180 are fertile and 153 hatch. Hatchability of fertile eggs is
Chicken eggs hatch after about
checkQuestions.explanation: The incubation period of the domestic fowl is 21 days.

checkQuestions.q: Egg turning in the incubator should stop at about day
checkQuestions.explanation: From day 18 the chick positions itself for hatching.

practicals.title: Detecting heat and calculating breeding dates
practicals.aim: To observe signs of heat (oestrus) in female farm animals and use oestrous cycle length and gestation periods to calculate breeding and parturition dates.
materials: Sows, does or cows on the school farm (or video)
Teaser male or boar for heat detection
safety: Keep a safe distance from boars and bulls; never enter a pen alone with a breeding male.
Wash hands after handling animals.
procedure: Observe the females twice daily (early morning and evening) for at least 30 minutes.

Record signs of heat: restlessness, mounting others, standing to be mounted, swollen reddened vulva, clear mucus discharge, frequent urination, reduced appetite; in sows, the standing reflex when pressure is applied on the back.
Record the date each animal is first seen on heat and the date of service.
Calculate the expected date of the next heat (in case service fails) using the cycle length.
Calculate the expected date of parturition using the gestation period.
Enter all dates on the breeding record card.
practicals.expectedObservations: An animal on heat is restless, bellows or grunts, has a swollen red vulva with mucus and stands still when mounted. Approximate cycle length: cow, sow, doe about 21 days; ewe about 17 days; rabbit is an induced ovulator. Gestation: cow ~283 days, sow ~114 days (3 months 3 weeks 3 days), goat/ewe ~150 days, rabbit ~31 days.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a sow is served on 10 March 2026. Next heat if not pregnant = 10 March + 21 days = 31 March 2026. Expected farrowing = 10 March + 114 days = 2 July 2026 (count: 21 days left in March, 30 in April → 51, 31 in May → 82, 30 in June → 112, plus 2 days → 2 July).
precautions: Observe at the same times each day so heat is not missed.
Use the exact date of service, not the date heat was first noticed, for gestation calculations.
sourcesOfError: Silent heat (no visible signs) leads to missed records.
Gestation length varies by a few days with breed and litter size.
commonMistakes: Counting the day of service as day 1, making the date one day early.
Using the cow's gestation period for a goat.
examTips: Show the month-by-month day count when calculating dates.
List at least three signs of heat for full marks; 'standing to be mounted' is the most reliable.

checkQuestions.q: The most reliable sign that a cow is on heat is that she
checkQuestions.explanation: Standing heat is the best indicator of oestrus.

checkQuestions.q: The gestation period of the sow is about
checkQuestions.explanation: Three months, three weeks and three days ≈ 114 days.

checkQuestions.q: A doe was served on 1 June. With a 150-day gestation, she should kid on about
checkQuestions.explanation: June 29 + July 31 + Aug 31 + Sep 30 + Oct 29 = 150 days → 29 October.

practicals.title: Routine management practices: identification, debeaking and castration
practicals.aim: To carry out or demonstrate routine management practices — ear-notching, ear-tagging, debeaking, castration, dehorning and hoof trimming — and to read an ear-notch number.
materials: Piglets, kids or chicks on the school farm
safety: Restrain animals firmly and gently; one person holds while another operates.
Disinfect tools between animals.
Only the teacher or farm attendant should use the hot debeaker or dehorning iron.
procedure: Restrain the animal appropriately (hold piglets by the hind legs, kids between the knees, chicks in the palm).
Ear-notching: using the key provided, cut V-shaped notches at the correct positions on the ear edges; apply antiseptic.
Debeaking: remove about one-third of the upper beak of 7–10-day-old chicks with a hot blade to prevent cannibalism.
Castration: apply an elastrator ring above the testes of a young kid or lamb, or use the Burdizzo on each spermatic cord separately.
Dehorning/disbudding: cauterise the horn buds of kids or calves within the first two weeks of life.
Record each practice, the date and the animal's identity in the farm register.
practicals.expectedObservations: Notched ears heal within a few days; debeaked chicks resume feeding within hours; the scrotum below an elastrator ring shrivels and drops off in about 2–3 weeks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Reading an ear notch using the key provided (example key: right ear lower edge = 1, right ear upper edge = 3, left ear lower edge = 10, left ear upper edge = 30, right ear tip = 100). Worked example: a piglet has 2 notches on the right lower edge (2 × 1 = 2), 1 on the right upper edge (3) and 1 on the left lower edge (10). Number = 2 + 3 + 10 = 15.
precautions: Carry out operations when animals are young to reduce stress and bleeding.
Avoid operations in very hot weather or during fly season, or apply fly repellent.
Do not notch too close to other notches or the ear may tear.
sourcesOfError: Notches cut in the wrong position give a wrong number.
Partial crushing of the cord leads to failed castration.
commonMistakes: Debeaking too much (cutting to the nostrils) so birds cannot eat.
Castrating an adult male without veterinary help.
examTips: Always state the reason for each practice (e.g. debeaking prevents feather pecking and cannibalism).
Use the key given in the question; ear-notch systems differ from farm to farm.
Mention the appropriate age for each operation.

checkQuestions.q: Debeaking of poultry is done mainly to
checkQuestions.explanation: Trimming the upper beak reduces injurious pecking.

checkQuestions.q: Using the key right lower = 1, right upper = 3, left lower = 10, a pig with 1 right lower and 2 left lower notches is number
The elastrator castrates by
options: cutting off blood supply with a rubber ring
checkQuestions.explanation: The tight ring stops blood flow so the scrotum withers.

checkQuestions.q: A permanent method of identifying a pig that leaves no external attachment is
checkQuestions.explanation: Notches are permanent and nothing can fall off.

practicals.title: Identifying feedstuffs and determining dry matter
practicals.aim: To identify common feed ingredients and non-conventional feeds, state the main nutrient each supplies, and determine the dry matter and moisture content of a forage.
safety: Use tongs to remove hot trays from the oven.
Avoid breathing in fine premix or fish meal dust.
Do not taste feeds.
procedure: Examine each feed sample; note colour, smell, texture and particle size.
Name each sample and classify it as energy feed, protein concentrate, mineral, vitamin supplement, roughage or non-conventional feed.
Weigh an empty dry tray, add about 200 g of freshly chopped grass and reweigh.
Dry the grass in the oven at about 105 °C, cool in a desiccator and weigh; repeat drying until the mass is constant.
Calculate the dry matter and moisture percentages.
Record all results in a table: feed, class, main nutrient, livestock it is fed to.
practicals.expectedObservations: Fish meal is brown with a strong fishy smell; groundnut cake is brown and flaky; maize is yellow or white grain; oyster shell is hard, white and flaky; bone meal is a white powder; premix is a fine coloured powder. Fresh young grass loses about three-quarters of its mass on drying.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Dry matter % = dry mass ÷ fresh mass × 100; moisture % = 100 − DM %. Worked example: 200 g of fresh grass gives 50 g after drying to constant mass. DM = 50 ÷ 200 × 100 = 25 %; moisture = 75 %.
precautions: Dry to constant mass so all water is removed.
Cool samples in a desiccator before weighing so they do not absorb moisture.
Chop forage finely for even drying.
sourcesOfError: Volatile compounds lost on drying.
Reabsorption of moisture before weighing.
Balance not tared.
commonMistakes: Classifying groundnut cake as an energy feed (it is a protein concentrate).
Using dry mass as the denominator.
examTips: Name the main nutrient: maize – carbohydrate/energy; fish meal – protein; oyster shell – calcium.
Show the subtraction of tray mass if the tray is weighed with the sample.

checkQuestions.q: Which feedstuff is mainly a source of calcium for laying hens?
checkQuestions.explanation: Oyster shell is almost pure calcium carbonate, needed for eggshells.

checkQuestions.q: Fresh forage weighing 400 g gives 120 g after oven drying. Its moisture content is
checkQuestions.explanation: DM = 30 %, so moisture = 70 %.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a non-conventional feed?
checkQuestions.explanation: Cassava peel is a farm by-product not traditionally used in commercial feed.

checkQuestions.q: Premix is added to rations to supply
checkQuestions.explanation: Premix contains vitamins and trace minerals in small amounts.

practicals.title: Formulating a ration with the Pearson square
practicals.aim: To formulate a livestock ration of a required crude protein level from two ingredients using the Pearson square, and to mix it.
apparatus: Mixing tray or clean concrete floor
safety: Wear a dust mask when mixing dry feeds.
Lift heavy bags with a straight back.
procedure: Write down the crude protein (CP) content of each ingredient and the required CP of the ration (e.g. 18 % for a broiler grower).
Draw a square; write the required CP in the centre, maize CP at the top left and groundnut cake CP at the bottom left.
Subtract diagonally, ignoring signs: the differences on the right give the parts of each ingredient.
Convert parts to percentages and then to kilograms for the batch size.
Weigh the ingredients, mix small items (premix, salt) with a little maize first, then mix everything thoroughly.
Check the answer by calculating the CP of the mixture.
practicals.expectedObservations: The finished mash is evenly coloured with no lumps of cake or pockets of premix.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: make 100 kg of 18 % CP feed from maize (9 %) and groundnut cake (45 %). Maize parts = 45 − 18 = 27; GNC parts = 18 − 9 = 9; total = 36. Maize = 27 ÷ 36 × 100 = 75 % → 75 kg; GNC = 9 ÷ 36 × 100 = 25 % → 25 kg. Check: 0.75 × 9 + 0.25 × 45 = 6.75 + 11.25 = 18 % CP.
precautions: The required CP must lie between the CP values of the two ingredients.
Premix and salt must be pre-mixed to spread evenly.
Use fresh, mould-free ingredients (aflatoxin risk in groundnut cake).
sourcesOfError: Actual nutrient values of local ingredients differ from table values.
Incomplete mixing.
commonMistakes: Subtracting across the same row instead of diagonally.
Forgetting to convert parts to percentages before finding kilograms.
examTips: Draw the square neatly — marks are awarded for the diagram as well as the answer.
Always verify by back-calculation.
State the class of animal the ration is meant for.

checkQuestions.q: To make a 20 % CP ration from maize (10 %) and soya bean meal (40 %), the parts of maize are
checkQuestions.explanation: Maize parts = 40 − 20 = 20; soya parts = 20 − 10 = 10.

checkQuestions.q: In the example above, the percentage of soya bean meal in the mix is
The Pearson square cannot be used to make a 50 % CP feed from maize (9 %) and GNC (45 %) because
options: 50 lies outside the range of the two ingredients
checkQuestions.explanation: The target must lie between the two ingredient values.

checkQuestions.q: A broiler starter ration usually contains about
checkQuestions.explanation: Young broilers need high-protein starter feed.

practicals.title: Feeding trial and feed conversion ratio
practicals.topic: Animal feeds and feeding: livestock rations
practicals.aim: To feed a group of broilers a known ration, record feed intake and weight gain, and calculate the feed conversion ratio (FCR).
safety: Disinfect footwear at the pen entrance (foot dip).
Wash hands after handling birds and litter.
procedure: Weigh the birds individually at the start and record the mean initial weight.
Weigh the feed given each day and the feed left over the next morning.
Weigh the birds weekly at the same time of day.
At the end of the trial, calculate total feed eaten per bird and total weight gain per bird.
Calculate FCR and plot mean body weight against age.
Compare the FCR with the standard for the breed.
practicals.expectedObservations: Weight increases slowly in the first week and then rapidly; the growth curve is S-shaped; well-managed broilers reach about 2 kg in 6 weeks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: FCR = feed consumed ÷ weight gain. Worked example: a broiler eats 4.2 kg of feed and grows from 0.04 kg to 2.04 kg (gain = 2.0 kg). FCR = 4.2 ÷ 2.0 = 2.1, meaning 2.1 kg of feed produced 1 kg of live weight. A lower FCR indicates better efficiency.
precautions: Subtract feed wasted or left over from feed offered.
Weigh birds before feeding to avoid gut-fill errors.
Keep water available at all times.
sourcesOfError: Spilt feed counted as eaten.
Mortality during the trial not accounted for.
commonMistakes: Dividing weight gain by feed (gives feed efficiency, not FCR).
Using final weight instead of weight gain.
examTips: State that a low FCR is desirable.
Show units in each step even though FCR itself has no unit.
Plot time on the x-axis and weight on the y-axis, with a title.

checkQuestions.q: A pig gains 30 kg after eating 90 kg of feed. Its FCR is
Which FCR shows the most efficient birds?
checkQuestions.explanation: Less feed is needed per kg of gain.

practicals.title: Identifying pasture and forage crops and estimating carrying capacity
practicals.aim: To identify common pasture grasses and legumes, estimate forage yield with a quadrat, and calculate how many animals a pasture can support.
materials: Pasture plot containing e.g. Guinea grass (Panicum maximum), Elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum), Giant star grass (Cynodon), Centro (Centrosema pubescens), Stylo (Stylosanthes), Calopo, Leucaena
safety: Wear boots against snakes and thorns.
Carry cutlasses pointing downwards.
procedure: Walk through the pasture and identify the grasses (narrow leaves, parallel veins, fibrous roots) and legumes (broad, compound leaves, root nodules).
Throw the quadrat randomly at least five times; cut all forage inside it at about 5 cm above ground.
Weigh the fresh forage from each throw and find the mean.
Dry a sub-sample to find the dry matter percentage.
Convert the mean yield to kg per hectare.
Calculate how many animals the pasture can support for a given grazing period.
practicals.expectedObservations: Grasses form tufts or creeping mats; legumes have trifoliate or pinnate leaves and pink root nodules; Elephant grass is tall with hairy leaf sheaths; Centro is a twining legume with purple flowers.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: mean fresh yield = 0.8 kg per m² → 0.8 × 10 000 = 8 000 kg/ha fresh. At 25 % DM → 2 000 kg DM/ha. Allowing 50 % utilisation → 1 000 kg DM usable. A 400 kg cow eats 2.5 % of body weight in DM = 10 kg/day, so the hectare gives 1 000 ÷ 10 = 100 cow-days. For a 30-day grazing period, it supports 100 ÷ 30 ≈ 3.3 cows (stocking rate about 3 cows per ha).
precautions: Throw the quadrat randomly to avoid bias.
Cut at a uniform height.
Weigh samples immediately to avoid moisture loss.
sourcesOfError: Too few quadrat throws for an uneven pasture.
Intake and utilisation figures are estimates.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that 1 ha = 10 000 m².
Using fresh rather than dry matter yield with DM intake figures.
examTips: Give both common and botanical names of forage species.
State uses: grazing, hay, silage, soil cover, nitrogen fixation (legumes).
Round animal numbers down in practice — you cannot keep part of a cow.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a forage legume?
checkQuestions.explanation: Centro is a legume; the others are grasses.

checkQuestions.q: A quadrat mean of 0.5 kg/m² equals
Legumes are valuable in pasture because they
options: fix nitrogen and are rich in protein
checkQuestions.explanation: Rhizobium in root nodules fixes nitrogen; the leaves are protein-rich.

checkQuestions.q: Silage is made by
options: fermenting green forage in an airtight silo
checkQuestions.explanation: Anaerobic fermentation produces lactic acid that preserves the forage.

practicals.title: Making hay and silage
practicals.aim: To conserve surplus forage as hay and silage and to calculate the capacity of a silage pit.
materials: Young green forage (e.g. Guinea grass, maize at milk stage)
Sand or old tyres for weighting
safety: Do not enter a closed silo or deep pit immediately after opening — gases can collect.
Handle cutlasses with care.
procedure: Hay: cut forage at early flowering, spread it thinly in the sun, turn it regularly until it is dry and brittle (about 15–20 % moisture), then bale or stack it under a roof.
Silage: cut forage at the right stage, wilt for a few hours and chop it into short pieces.
Measure the pit and line it with polythene.
Fill the pit in layers, sprinkling diluted molasses on each layer, and compact each layer firmly to remove air.
Cover with polythene and weight it down with soil or tyres to make it airtight.
Open after about 3–6 weeks and assess colour, smell and texture.
practicals.expectedObservations: Good hay is green, leafy, sweet-smelling and free of mould. Good silage is yellow-green to olive, firm, with a pleasant sour (vinegar-like) smell; poor silage is dark, slimy and smells of rotten eggs or ammonia.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Silo volume = length × width × depth. Worked example: pit 4 m × 2 m × 1.5 m = 12 m³. At a packed density of 600 kg/m³ the pit holds 12 × 600 = 7 200 kg of silage. A cow fed 20 kg/day uses 7 200 ÷ 20 = 360 cow-days, i.e. 10 cows for 36 days.
precautions: Exclude air by thorough compaction and sealing; air causes moulding.
Do not make hay in rainy weather.
Cut at the correct stage of growth for quality.
sourcesOfError: Density depends on compaction and moisture.
Spoilage at the top and sides reduces usable silage.
commonMistakes: Saying silage is dried forage (that is hay).
Leaving air pockets when filling the silo.
examTips: State that silage making is anaerobic fermentation producing lactic acid.
List qualities of good hay and good silage — commonly asked.
Show the volume, mass and days in separate steps.

checkQuestions.q: The acid that preserves good silage is mainly
checkQuestions.explanation: Lactic acid bacteria lower the pH and preserve the forage.

checkQuestions.q: A silo 3 m × 2 m × 2 m filled at 500 kg/m³ holds
checkQuestions.explanation: Volume 12 m³ × 500 = 6 000 kg.

checkQuestions.q: Silage with a rotten-egg smell indicates
options: too much air or poor fermentation
checkQuestions.explanation: Butyric and putrefactive fermentation give foul smells.

checkQuestions.q: The main aim of hay and silage making is to
options: conserve forage for the dry season
checkQuestions.explanation: Conserved forage feeds animals when pasture is scarce.

practicals.title: Artificial insemination: equipment and semen processing
practicals.aim: To identify AI equipment and their uses, describe semen collection, evaluation, dilution and storage, and calculate the number of insemination doses from an ejaculate.
materials: Pictures or video of collection and insemination
safety: Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C) causes severe cold burns; use gloves and goggles.
Wear arm-length gloves for rectal palpation.
Restrain the female in a crush.
procedure: Identify each item of AI equipment and state its use.
Collection: the artificial vagina, warmed to about 42 °C and lubricated, is used to collect semen from a bull mounting a teaser.
Evaluation: examine the semen under the microscope for volume, colour, concentration and motility; reject samples with low motility.
Dilution: add diluent to extend the semen into many doses and fill straws.
Storage: freeze straws and store them in liquid nitrogen.
Insemination: thaw the straw in water at about 35–37 °C, load the gun and deposit the semen into the cervix or uterine body of a cow in standing heat, guided by a hand in the rectum.
practicals.expectedObservations: Good bull semen is creamy-white with strong mass motion (wave-like swirling) under low power.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: ejaculate volume 5 mL with 1.2 × 10⁹ sperm/mL → total 6 × 10⁹ sperm; motility 70 % → 4.2 × 10⁹ motile sperm. At 20 × 10⁶ motile sperm per dose, doses = 4.2 × 10⁹ ÷ 2 × 10⁷ = 210 doses. With 0.5 mL straws, total volume = 210 × 0.5 = 105 mL, so diluent needed = 105 − 5 = 100 mL.
precautions: Avoid cold shock — keep semen at body temperature until diluted.
Inseminate at the correct time (about 12 hours after onset of standing heat).
Sterilise all equipment.
sourcesOfError: Estimation of motility under the microscope is subjective.
Some sperm die during freezing and thawing.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply by motility percentage.
Confusing the artificial vagina (collection) with the insemination gun.
examTips: Give at least three advantages of AI: wide use of superior sires, disease control, no need to keep bulls, semen can be stored for years.
Show powers of ten clearly in calculations.

checkQuestions.q: Frozen semen is stored in
checkQuestions.explanation: Liquid nitrogen keeps sperm viable for many years.

checkQuestions.q: The artificial vagina is used for
checkQuestions.explanation: It imitates the vagina so the bull ejaculates into a collection tube.

checkQuestions.q: An ejaculate contains 3 × 10⁹ motile sperm. At 1.5 × 10⁷ per dose, the number of doses is
An advantage of AI over natural mating is that
options: semen of a superior bull can serve many cows
checkQuestions.explanation: One ejaculate can inseminate hundreds of cows.

practicals.title: Identifying livestock parasites and preparing an acaricide dip
practicals.aim: To identify common ecto- and endoparasites of farm animals, state their effects and control, and prepare an acaricide dip of the correct concentration.
materials: Preserved tapeworm, liver fluke and roundworm (Ascaris)
safety: Acaricides are poisonous: wear gloves, goggles and a mask; do not eat or drink while handling them.
Dispose of used dip away from wells and streams.
procedure: Examine each parasite with a hand lens; note size, body divisions, legs, suckers or hooks.
Classify each as ectoparasite (lives on the host) or endoparasite (lives inside).
Draw and label a tick and a tapeworm scolex.
State the host, site, damage and control of each parasite.
Read the acaricide label and calculate the volume of concentrate needed for the dip.
Measure the concentrate, add it to the water and stir well.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ticks are oval with eight legs (adult) and no body division; lice are small, flattened and six-legged; the tapeworm is long, flat and segmented with a scolex bearing hooks and suckers; the liver fluke is leaf-shaped with two suckers; Ascaris is a long, cylindrical, unsegmented worm.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂. Worked example: concentrate 12.5 %, required dip 0.05 %, dip volume 200 L. V₁ = 0.05 × 200 ÷ 12.5 = 0.8 L (800 mL) of concentrate made up to 200 L with water.
precautions: Use exactly the recommended concentration — too weak gives resistance; too strong poisons animals.
Dip animals in the cool of the day and after watering them so they do not drink the dip.
Keep preserved specimens in labelled bottles.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate measurement of small volumes of concentrate.
Evaporation increases dip concentration over time.
commonMistakes: Calling ticks insects (they are arachnids with eight legs).
Adding the concentrate after only part of the water and not topping up.
examTips: Give the life cycle of the liver fluke with the snail as the intermediate host — often asked.
Name a specific disease transmitted, e.g. ticks transmit heartwater and babesiosis (redwater).
Write the dilution formula before substituting.

checkQuestions.q: Which parasite needs a water snail as an intermediate host?
checkQuestions.explanation: Fasciola develops in Lymnaea snails.

checkQuestions.q: How much 20 % concentrate is needed to make 100 L of 0.1 % dip?
An adult tick has
checkQuestions.explanation: Ticks are arachnids.

checkQuestions.q: Drenching is a method of controlling
checkQuestions.explanation: Drenching gives an anthelmintic by mouth.

practicals.title: Field and storage pests of farm animals and their feeds
practicals.aim: To identify field pests (e.g. tsetse fly, mosquito, rats, blackfly) and storage pests of feeds (e.g. maize weevil, rats, moths), state their economic importance and estimate the level of feed damage.
materials: Preserved tsetse fly, house fly, mosquito, cockroach
safety: Handle infested grain with gloves and wash hands; mouldy grain may carry aflatoxin.
Do not handle rat droppings with bare hands (Lassa fever risk).
procedure: Examine each pest and note distinguishing features (e.g. tsetse fly wings fold like closed scissors over the back; weevil has a long snout).
Classify pests as field pests (attack animals) or storage pests (attack feed or stored products).
Count 200 grains from an infested maize sample and sort them into damaged (holed) and undamaged grains.
Calculate the percentage infestation.
State the damage done by each pest and appropriate control measures.
practicals.expectedObservations: Damaged grains have round exit holes and powdery frass; the tsetse fly has a forward-pointing proboscis and a hatchet-shaped cell in the wing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Percentage infestation = damaged grains ÷ total grains × 100. Worked example: 36 of 200 grains are holed: 36 ÷ 200 × 100 = 18 % infestation.
precautions: Pick grains at random from the sample.
Seal infested samples to prevent spread to other stores.
sourcesOfError: Hidden infestation inside grains without exit holes.
Non-random sampling.
commonMistakes: Confusing pests with parasites — parasites live on/in the host; pests damage or annoy animals or stored products.
Giving 'use chemicals' without naming a method.
examTips: Give the economic importance in specific terms, e.g. tsetse flies transmit trypanosomiasis, which causes anaemia and loss of weight.
For storage pests, include hygiene, drying feed, proper storage and approved fumigants.

checkQuestions.q: The tsetse fly transmits
checkQuestions.explanation: Tsetse flies carry trypanosomes.

checkQuestions.q: In a sample of 250 grains, 40 are damaged. Infestation is
A storage pest of livestock feed is the
checkQuestions.explanation: Weevils bore into stored grain.

practicals.title: Clinical examination: temperature, pulse and respiration
practicals.topic: General symptoms of diseases in farm animals
practicals.aim: To examine a farm animal for signs of ill-health and measure rectal temperature, pulse rate and respiration rate.
safety: Restrain the animal firmly; stand to the side.
Disinfect the thermometer before and after use.
procedure: Observe the animal at rest: posture, appetite, coat, eyes, nostrils, faeces and behaviour.
Shake down the thermometer, lubricate it and insert it gently into the rectum, holding it against the rectal wall for about one minute; read and record.
Count the pulse at the femoral artery (inside the thigh) for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
Count flank movements for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get the respiration rate.
Compare the readings with normal ranges and list any signs of ill-health.
practicals.expectedObservations: A healthy goat is alert, has a smooth coat, bright eyes, moist muzzle, normal faeces, and temperature about 38.5–40 °C, pulse 70–90 per minute, respiration 15–30 per minute. A sick animal may be dull, isolated, off feed, with fever, diarrhoea, discharges or a rough coat.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: rectal temperature 41.2 °C; 22 pulse beats in 15 s → 22 × 4 = 88 beats/min; 9 flank movements in 15 s → 9 × 4 = 36 breaths/min. The temperature is above the normal range (fever) and the respiration rate is high, so the goat is likely to be sick.
precautions: Take readings when the animal is calm and has not just been chased.
Keep the thermometer in long enough for a steady reading.
Count carefully and use a stopwatch.
sourcesOfError: Excitement or heat stress raises pulse and respiration.
Thermometer not in contact with the rectal wall.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply 15-second counts by 4.
Taking oral temperature in animals.
examTips: Learn normal temperature ranges of cattle, goat, pig and fowl.
List general symptoms clearly: loss of appetite, dullness, fever, discharges, abnormal faeces, rough coat.

checkQuestions.q: 18 pulse beats are counted in 15 s. The pulse rate is
Which is a general sign of ill-health in livestock?
checkQuestions.explanation: Sick animals often stop eating.

checkQuestions.q: A goat's temperature of 41.5 °C indicates
checkQuestions.explanation: It is above the normal range of about 38.5–40 °C.

checkQuestions.q: The pulse of a goat is best felt at the
checkQuestions.explanation: The femoral artery lies close to the skin there.

practicals.title: Disease prevention: vaccination, drenching and farm sanitation
practicals.topic: Diseases of farm animals, prevention and control
practicals.aim: To demonstrate vaccination, drenching, spraying and farm sanitation and to calculate correct drug and vaccine quantities.
safety: Use one needle per animal or disinfect between animals; dispose of needles safely.
Wear gloves and a mask when spraying.
Never give drugs past their expiry date.
procedure: Weigh the animal or estimate its weight with a weigh band.
Calculate the dose from the label and draw it into the drenching gun.
Drench by holding the head level, inserting the nozzle at the corner of the mouth over the tongue and releasing slowly.
For poultry, reconstitute water-vaccine in chlorine-free cool water, withdraw drinking water for about 1–2 hours before, and give the vaccine water to be finished within 2 hours.
Clean and disinfect pens, drinkers and feeders; refill the foot dip at the pen entrance.
Record the date, product, dose and animals treated.
practicals.expectedObservations: Correctly drenched animals swallow without coughing; vaccinated birds should show protective immunity after 1–2 weeks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example (anthelmintic): dose 2.5 mL per 10 kg; goat = 32 kg → 32 ÷ 10 × 2.5 = 8 mL. Worked example (vaccine): 500 birds, vials of 100 doses → 500 ÷ 100 = 5 vials.
precautions: Keep vaccines cold (2–8 °C) and away from sunlight.
Do not use chlorinated tap water for water vaccines; chlorine kills live vaccine virus.
Drench slowly to avoid drug entering the lungs.
sourcesOfError: Guessing body weight leads to under- or over-dosing.
Birds not drinking evenly receive uneven vaccine doses.
commonMistakes: Under-dosing, which encourages drug resistance.
Mixing vaccines with hot or chlorinated water.
examTips: Distinguish prevention (vaccination, sanitation, quarantine) from treatment (drugs).
State storage conditions for vaccines.
Round up vials needed to a whole number.

checkQuestions.q: A sheep of 45 kg needs a drench at 1 mL per 5 kg. The dose is
How many 200-dose vials are needed for 900 birds?
checkQuestions.explanation: 4.5 vials rounds up to 5.

checkQuestions.q: Live poultry vaccines should not be mixed with chlorinated water because chlorine
checkQuestions.explanation: Chlorine inactivates live vaccine.

checkQuestions.q: A foot dip at a pen entrance helps to
options: prevent entry of disease organisms on footwear
checkQuestions.explanation: Disinfectant kills pathogens carried on boots.

practicals.title: Egg collection, grading, preservation and hen-day production
practicals.topic: Processing techniques for different farm animal products
practicals.aim: To collect, clean, grade and preserve eggs and to calculate the hen-day egg production of a laying flock.
materials: Vegetable oil or paraffin wax (for coating)
safety: Wash hands after handling eggs — shells may carry Salmonella.
Handle eggs gently.
procedure: Collect eggs at least three times daily and place them broad end up in trays.
Dry-clean soiled eggs with a slightly rough cloth; avoid washing with cold water.
Candle eggs to remove cracked eggs, blood spots and meat spots.
Weigh each egg and grade it by size (e.g. small, medium, large, extra-large).
Preserve eggs by refrigeration or by coating with oil to close the shell pores.
Use the record of eggs laid and number of hens to calculate hen-day production.
practicals.expectedObservations: Fresh eggs have a small air cell; oil-coated eggs keep longer because water loss and entry of microbes are reduced.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Hen-day production % = eggs laid ÷ (number of hens × number of days) × 100. Worked example: 80 hens lay 450 eggs in 7 days. Hen-days = 80 × 7 = 560. Production = 450 ÷ 560 × 100 = 80.4 %.
precautions: Store eggs broad end up to keep the air cell stable.
Keep eggs away from strong smells (they absorb odours).
Sell or use eggs in order of collection (first in, first out).
sourcesOfError: Uncounted broken or eaten eggs.
Changes in hen numbers due to mortality during the week.
commonMistakes: Dividing eggs by hens only and forgetting the number of days.
Washing eggs in cold water, which draws microbes into the shell.
examTips: List methods of preserving eggs: refrigeration, oiling, waxing, lime water.
Show hen-days as a separate step in the calculation.

checkQuestions.q: 100 hens lay 560 eggs in a week. Hen-day production is
Coating eggs with oil preserves them by
checkQuestions.explanation: Sealed pores reduce moisture loss and microbial entry.

checkQuestions.q: Eggs should be stored with the
checkQuestions.explanation: This keeps the air cell and yolk in place.
